stories.headline: Anthropic Researchers Resign, Warn AI Could Kill All Humans This Decade
stories.summary:
Three Anthropic researchers went public Tuesday with stark warnings about artificial intelligence development, with at least one resigning to sound the alarm. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon wrote on X after quitting that people building AI "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," and alleged that neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is acting ethically. A second senior Anthropic researcher who did not resign publicly stated there is more than a 10% chance AI "could kill all humans."

Coxon alleged that company executives and senior researchers deliberately couch their language for public audiences to appear measured, while privately expressing far more alarming views. He accused both Anthropic and OpenAI of being aware they are "gambling with our lives" by racing toward superintelligent AI capable of improving itself beyond human control. The warnings represent some of the most direct public statements from insiders at a leading AI safety-focused laboratory.

The disclosures carry particular weight because Anthropic has positioned itself as the safety-conscious alternative to competitors, making internal dissent from its own researchers a significant credibility challenge for the company. The episode adds to a growing chorus of concern from AI practitioners about the pace of development relative to safety guardrails. Anthropic has not yet issued a public response to the researchers' claims.

stories.headline: Update: Germany's Merz Confronts AfD in Bundestag After Party's Historic Saxony-Anhalt Victory
stories.summary:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz clashed sharply with AfD leader Alice Weidel in a stormy Bundestag session Wednesday following the far-right party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where it won nearly 44% of the vote. Merz called the AfD a "destructive force" and charged that its proposed "remigration" policy targeting irregular migrants would amount to "ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin," noting that one in six skilled workers in Germany has a migration background. AfD MPs heckled Merz so loudly that Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to expel members from the chamber.

Weidel countered that voters had repudiated Merz's coalition with the Social Democrats as a "total failure" and said mass migration had produced daily knife violence and attacks on public transport. She argued that Merz's conservatives had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, where they won just 17.2% of the vote — roughly half their previous result. The AfD fell three seats short of an outright majority in the state, leaving its path to forming a government uncertain; no far-right party has governed any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two.

Merz acknowledged the result was "seismic" and said it had changed Germany, but insisted the AfD had damaged German interests by backing Russia and would never achieve a national majority. U.S. President Donald Trump praised the AfD's result, saying the "Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night" and linking it to dissatisfaction with immigration policy. A scheduled phone call between Trump and Merz to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks was postponed Wednesday with no new date set, the German government confirmed.

stories.headline: Pentagon Upheaval Deepens as Hegseth Purges Military Leadership During Active Combat Operations
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's sweeping reorganization of Pentagon leadership is drawing bipartisan alarm as the United States simultaneously wages active military operations in the Gulf. The latest flashpoint is the resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, a senior civilian leader who clashed with Hegseth over the pace of military modernization. Driscoll had championed rapid integration of drone technology throughout Army formations, citing lessons from the Ukraine war, but sources say Hegseth blocked expansion of that agenda and dismissed the generals responsible for implementing it.

Retired officers and Republican critics have warned that the simultaneous hollowing-out of military leadership and prosecution of an active conflict risks U.S. readiness. Republican Senator Thom Tillis called for Hegseth to be fired, saying he had "never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country." Former National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster said Driscoll's departure was "not good news for our nation, for the army," and a retired Navy captain familiar with the situation said Hegseth had "hollowed out" military leadership at a critical moment.

Supporters of Hegseth and the Trump administration argue the Pentagon's civilian and military bureaucracy had grown bloated and resistant to reform, and that Hegseth is executing a mandate to cut waste and reimpose civilian control over a politicized institution. The tension reflects a broader debate over whether the administration's culture-war priorities at the Defense Department are compatible with managing complex combat operations stretching U.S. forces across the globe.

stories.headline: North Korea Builds New Two-Storey Uranium Enrichment Facility at Yongbyon, IAEA Warns
stories.summary:
North Korea has constructed a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed this week, describing it as a cause for "serious concern." The building is reportedly capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades used to enrich uranium, and the IAEA also reported that an expanded annex at a second enrichment site, in Kangson near Pyongyang, has begun operating. The agency relies on satellite imagery for its assessments, having been expelled from North Korea in 2009.

IAEA Director Rafael Grossi called the developments "clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions" and said they represented a continued and accelerating expansion of North Korea's sanctioned nuclear infrastructure. Kim Jong Un visited the Yongbyon facility in June and praised its "greatly expanded production capacity," saying it offered "the possibility of carrying out larger plans," according to earlier IAEA reporting. Analysts note that many North Korean nuclear facilities remain unknown and concealed, making the full scope of the program difficult to assess or target.

The findings underscore the steady growth of North Korea's nuclear arsenal under Kim, who has overseen a record number of missile tests including multiple intercontinental ballistic missile launches since 2017. North Korea has conducted six nuclear weapons tests, the last in September 2017. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung proposed talks in August on officially ending the Korean War, but Pyongyang has not responded publicly to the overture.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Military Destroys Five Iranian Oil Tankers as Brent Crude Hits $100
stories.summary:
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Tuesday, U.S. Central Command announced. The strikes were carried out in response to two separate Iranian ballistic missile attacks on U.S. Navy warships in as many days. The tankers destroyed were identified as the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, M/T Riesco, and a fifth vessel.

The escalation sent Brent crude oil surging past $100 per barrel for the first time since July, a significant threshold that amplifies pressure on global consumers and financial markets. Iran separately struck American-linked targets in Jordan, continuing a cycle of tit-for-tat strikes that has persisted throughout the now seven-month-old conflict. The Trump administration also announced new sanctions this week targeting 36 entities accused of supporting Iran's aviation sector to move weapons and personnel.

The widening conflict is raising fears of a sustained oil supply shock, with the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding shipping lanes increasingly contested. Analysts and market observers warn that sustained prices above $100 per barrel could accelerate inflation pressures in the United States and globally, complicating Federal Reserve monetary policy ahead of its September meeting. Iran denied U.S. accounts of some engagements, claiming it targeted three U.S.-linked ships.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Strikes Kyiv TV Station as Five Killed; Trump and Putin Speak by Phone
stories.summary:
Russian drones struck the Kyiv headquarters of Ukrainian television channel We Are Ukraine on Tuesday, injuring at least five people while journalists were broadcasting live, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced. The daytime attack followed overnight missile and drone strikes on the Ukrainian capital that killed three people and injured 25 others, damaging residential buildings across multiple districts. Zelensky called the media strike a "new page in Russian degradation" and renewed appeals to Western allies for support.

The attacks came just days after both countries agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals during a visit by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv, a ceasefire arrangement Russia appears to have abandoned. A BBC Verify analysis found Kyiv is now experiencing more daily air raid alerts than at any point since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022. A separate Russian strike on a passenger train in southern Ukraine killed a female employee.

In a significant diplomatic development Tuesday evening, Presidents Trump and Putin spoke by phone for approximately one hour in what Moscow described as "constructive and very frank" talks. The Trump administration declined to publicly comment on the call's substance, while Witkoff had earlier said "substantive progress was made" during the envoy visits without providing specifics. The talks have so far yielded no breakthrough on ending the conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Bans Canadian Alcohol, Dairy and Motorcycle Imports as Trade War Deepens
stories.summary:
President Trump signed a series of executive orders Tuesday banning U.S. imports of Canadian alcoholic spirits, certain dairy products and motorcycles, with the measures set to take effect September 29. Trump accused Canada of "discriminating" against American businesses by restricting U.S. goods while allowing the same products from other countries to enter freely. The announcement came hours after Canada's retaliatory tariffs on approximately $20 billion in U.S. goods took effect just after midnight.

Canada's trade minister Dominic LeBlanc called the new U.S. measures "unjustified" and said he would work to protect Canadian workers and businesses, adding that he had contacted his American counterpart and pledged to engage "in good faith." Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney acknowledged that diversifying away from the U.S. as Canada's largest trading partner "will come at a cost." Canada's counter-tariffs match U.S. duties and target dairy, steel, clothing and furniture, among other goods.

Economists note the import ban covers only about 0.25 percent of Canada's total exports to the U.S., but Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said Trump's willingness to impose an outright ban signals the measures are "about inflicting economic pain rather than raising revenue." No new negotiations have been scheduled since talks collapsed in late August. The escalating dispute is creating political headaches for Republican Senate candidates who must defend the administration's economic record while distancing themselves from tariffs targeting key Canadian imports.

stories.headline: Update: UK Sanctions Israeli Settlements, Israel Shuts British Consulate in Jerusalem
stories.summary:
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that the UK would ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, framing the move as an effort to "deter settlement expansion" and block development of the contested E1 site east of Jerusalem. Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of conducting the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians and said the Israeli government had turned a "blind eye." Israel has issued tenders for approximately 1,200 settlement homes at the E1 site.

Israel responded swiftly and sharply, with Foreign Minister Gideon Saar announcing the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and calling the UK government "hostile." The UK's chief rabbi separately claimed British Jews would be less safe as a result of the sanctions, a charge Miliband rejected. The coordinated nature of the Western action — the UK, France and Canada all moved against settlement goods — was designed to spread diplomatic risk, though Israel's retaliation focused primarily on Britain.

Supporters of the sanctions argue they apply meaningful economic pressure on settlement expansion that has accelerated during the Gaza conflict, while critics, including Israeli officials, contend the measures are one-sided and will damage relations with a key regional partner. Palestinians strongly backed the import ban. The dispute marks a significant deterioration in UK-Israel relations and adds Britain to a growing list of Western governments publicly breaking with Israeli settlement policy.
